For teamworks, it will be verified that each member of the group master all the work in its entirety and explicit parts that he personally developed. The evaluation is on 0-30 scale and the mark is communicated to the student at the end of the oral exam. The final mark is the average of written and oral marks. “30 cum laude” is given to students who achieve the highest score on each item and use precise vocabulary.

sections.Learning objectives: The student knows and understands the information required to design and conduct experimental investigations in the laboratory or wind tunnel; He/she is able to acquire knowledge independently concerning the principles and applications of innovative techniques in the field of fluid dynamics which have been successfully developed in recent years; Is able to analyse, interpret and critically evaluate the results of experiments with independent judgement; He/she is able to find the necessary information to tackle new problems and to design the experiment as a whole according to the investigation and the results to be obtained.
sections.Prerequisites: It is advisable to have passed the Fluid Mechanics exam.
sections.Course unit content: The course aims to provide students with the tools to study the interaction between wind and the bodies it impacts. Models of wind generation and characteristics are analysed on the basis of the physics of the atmosphere, with a description of the statistics used to describe the random velocity field that develops in the Earth's atmospheric boundary layer. The fluid-dynamic aspects induced by the presence of bodies immersed in the fluid vein of elongated or squat geometry are then analysed, defining the fundamental parameters governing the physical phenomenon. The similarity criteria adopted for wind tunnel modelling are introduced, with a description of the different types of wind tunnels. The measuring instruments used are introduced and described. Finally, the analytical and numerical models most frequently adopted in CFD are introduced.

sections.Learning objectives: Knowledge and understanding The modern manufacturing companies have to develop new or improved products, at a competitive cost and in ashorter time to market. In this context, at the end of the course the student will know a structured approach and modern methods to do thiswithin a company, knowing how to address best the development of a new product depending on its features. Applying knowledge and understanding. The student will develop a new product, accounting for market needs, the products / platforms from which to start, competing products, the processes to be implemented within the enterprise and internal/external resources to be committed. He will know how to choose the architecture to be given to the product and to evaluate the number of units sold according to the concept developed, associating an assessment of the industrial cost. Making judgments Students will be able to identify market opportunities for new products, evaluate product development, product structure, and business objectives between the market-pull and alternative (tecnology-push, custom, or platform) ), generate and select conceptual alternatives in a rational manner, taking into account the suitable performance compromises and verifying the sales potential of the product developed. Communication skills It is expected that, at the end of the course, the student will be able to transmit,in oral, written and graphical form, the process of developing a new product applied concretely to a case identified and assigned at the beginning of the course. Students must communicate their knowledge through appropriate means such as animated presentations, 3D CAD drawings, tables, diagrams, flow diagrams, and numerical spreadsheets. Learning ability The student who has attended the course will be able to deepen his / her knowledge of new product development methodologies through the autonomous consultation of specialized texts, scientific journals or dissertations, even outside lecture topics, to effectively tackle job placement or to undertake further training paths.
sections.Prerequisites: The knowledge of the mechanical technology / manufacturing technologies is useful, although not mandatory
sections.Course unit content: The course presents and applies in a concrete case, the structure of the product design and product development process and the methodologies that can be used for this purpose in the enterprises
sections.Full programme: The course is divided into the following lectures: - Introduction to the product design and development process; - Organization and management of development projects; - Planning of the product; ¬ Identification of customer needs; - Definition of product specifications; ¬ Quality Function Deployment (QFD) and House of Quality (HOQ) in product design and development; - Conceptual design: generation and selection of ideas; - Testing of the concept; - Architecture of the product; - Role of the industrial design; - Design for assembly; - Prototyping. Lectures are alternated with lab classes on the use of 3D CAD in product development (SolidWorks software) for the desing of parts and assemblies
sections.Bibliography: Ulrich K.T., Eppinger S.D., Product design and development, McGraw- Hill,5° Ed., 2011. The slides displayed during the course are made available to students in PDF format along with other course materials (Word templates, Excel spreadsheets) on the Elly platform, after the student has enroled to the course
sections.Teaching methods: The course has a weight of 6 CFU, which corresponds to 42 hours of frontal lesson. Didactic activities will be conducted by focusing on frontal classroom lessons with the help of PowerPoint slides, alternating with laboratory exercises on the use of CAD 3D (SolidWorks software). During the frontal lessons, the course topics from a theoretical point of view are presented. At the end of each lesson, students are asked a question whose elaboration and solution is discussed collectively in the classroom the next time. For processing and solving the question, students can use personal computing tools such as computers, tablets / smartphones connected to the internet
sections.Assessment methods and criteria: The exam consists of the oral presentation and discussion of the project of development of an innovative product. The identification of the product to be developed is carried out by students by the third lesson of the course, possibly taking advantage of the suggestions given by the teacher. The project includes: report in Word, PowerPoint presentation (maximum duration 25 min), 3D CAD drawings of the product developed. The project ends at the stage of embodiment design, which defines the concept of a product, its architecture, materials and production technology, but not detail drawings with the dimensions and the final form (industrialization). The evaluation, up to the score of 30/30 and Lode, is made based on the presence of the above elements, the comprehensiveness of the development activities shown in the classroom, the consistency and completeness of the description of the activities performed

sections.Learning objectives: Knowledge and understanding: At the end of the course the student will integrate his knowledge of base chemistry with the typical application of mechanical engineering, will have a complete overview of materials for industrial engineering in relation to their chemical composition, their structure and characteristics of use. Applying knowledge and understanding: At the end of the course of study the student will develop the ability to choose the best material for the desired applications. He will be able to predict physical and chemical processing to be implemented on materials in order to modify the structure to improve its properties. He will also be able to put in place the appropriate measures to prolong the life of the material. The student will also be able to predict the controls to be carried out to verify that the materials used meet the desired characteristics. Making judgments: On passing the exam, the student should have developed the ability to critically evaluate the analytical data of the mechanical behavior of a material to predict the behavior in work, as well as the ability to interpret the data of the controls for acceptance of a material to be used. Communication skills: On passing the exam, the student should have acquired sufficient command of the language, at least as regards the technical terminology and specific chemical teaching. Learning skills: The final seminar activities are designed to introduce students to the latest developments in terms of research in the field of materials science applied to civil engineering: the student should have acquired the knowledge and basic skills of discipline to deal with, in the future, an independent deepening of these aspects.

sections.Learning objectives: At the end of the course the student will have acquired - knowledge relating to the design of the experimentation (even virtual) on Energy Systems and the interpretation of the obtained results; - skills concerning the numerical and experimental characterization of Energy Systems operations; - tools for the implementation, execution and analysis of models for the simulation of Energy Systems and for the interpretation of simulation results.
sections.Prerequisites: A basic knowledge of fundamentals of Mathematics, Physics Thermodynamics, Fluid Mechanics and Energy Systems is required.
sections.Course unit content: The course is a complement to the theoretical contents presented in the Energy Systems AB (I Module) course, which is held in the first semester. During the course, energy conversion systems (turbogas, steam plants and internal combustion engines) and their components will be analyzed with IT tools in order to determine their performance as the operating conditions vary. The main problems related to the experimental characterization of energy systems and fluid machines will also be analysed in this framework.
sections.Full programme: The course is divided into two parts. The first part analyzes the equipment required for experimentation, with a particular focus on the instruments and sensors typically used in test cells, the measurements acquired, and signal processing. Emphasis is placed on the procedures needed to perform test‑bench experiments under both steady‑state and transient conditions. The second part of the course focuses on the use of virtual environments for the simulation and modeling of energy systems. Specifically, several exercises will be proposed to numerically solve engineering problems through physical–mathematical modeling (calculation of thermodynamic transformations, analysis of energy systems). The models developed will then be used to investigate the effect of the main control parameters on system performance; in this way, students will be able to understand their impact through virtual experimentation of the system under study. These data will subsequently be used to generate reports that clearly and technically present the results of the analyses performed.

sections.Learning objectives: Knowledge and understanding: At the end of this course the student should know the basics of machine design. He should gain understanding of the many factors affecting the design of mechanical parts with special regards to safety and reliability. He should be familiar with design schemes and checks required to analyze machine parts. Applying knowledge and understanding: He should be able to design a mechanical part on the basis of suitable material and process selection, load analysis and functional requirements. He should be able to select from catalogues the main mechanical components found in machines. He should be able to draw and dimension the part for production. Making judgments: By the end of the course the student should be able to critically analyze machines and mechanical components and to their functions and requisites. Communication skills: The student should be able to clearly present the functioning of mechanical devices and the design issues involved.
sections.Prerequisites: It will be very useful to recall the following concepts: - Physics 1: units of measurement, forces and moments in a plane, vector representation, graphical resolution of static equilibrium - Machine drawing: views, dimensioning, dimensional and geometric tolerances, bearing assembly - Mechanical technology: machining technologies, heat treatment of steel - Metallurgy: metal alloys and their applications, mechanical testing - Structural science: beam theory, mass geometry, de Saint-Venant theory - Rational mechanics: kinematics, rigid body dynamics, kinematic mechanisms, and force calculations
sections.Course unit content: The course covers the principles of mechanical design applied to machine components, starting with the strength characteristics of commonly used materials and the concept of safety. It then introduces methods and models for the schematization of acting loads and the calculation and sizing of components. A key aspect is the introduction to strength testing under fatigue loads.
sections.Full programme: Introduction to Construction Design, Safety, Factor of Safety with Statistical Reliability Concepts, Technical Standards, Mechanical Testing of Materials, Tensile, Hardness, Impact, Fatigue, Fracture Testing, Metallic Materials (Steel, Cast Iron, Aluminum, Magnesium, Titanium Alloys), Non-Metallic Materials (Polymers and Ceramics), Manufacturing Technologies, Selection Criteria. Load Analysis, Equilibrium, Application of the Beam Model in Mechanics, Normal Force, Bending, Shear, and Torsion. Stresses and Strains. Mohr Circles. Principal Stresses, Strength Criteria (Tresca, Von Mises, Rankine), Ductility and Brittleness. Compressive Buckling and Eulerian Loading. Stiffness. Highly Curvatured Beams. Notched Geometries, Nominal and Local Stresses, Stress Concentration Factor Kt. Conformal and Non-Conformal Contact, Specific Contact Pressure, Hertzian Theory, Stresses in Contact between Elementary Bodies. Thermal Expansion. Fatigue of Metallic Materials, Characteristics of the Phenomenon, Fatigue Testing, Stress Limit fatigue, S/N curves, fatigue parameter estimates, influence factors, mean stress effect, fatigue damage accumulation, multiaxial stress effect, notch sensitivity, Notch effect factor Kf. Contact fatigue, pitting, fretting.

sections.Teaching methods: Course topics are presented through lectures and numerical exercises carried out in the classroom. Problems are proposed to be carried out at home with subsequent discussion in the classroom. Groups of students are also stimulated to analyse and study a real mechanical device.
sections.Assessment methods and criteria: The examination consists of a written test, which must be passed with a minimum score of 18/30, followed by an oral test. In the written exam, students will be required to solve an exercise concerning the design of a simple mechanical system, such as a lifting device, a pressure vessel or a drive shaft, considering the main factors that determine the safety of the system, such as the choice of the most suitable materials, durability, or compliance with regulations. In order to pass the written exam, it is essential to correctly perform the load analysis by means of static resolution and the determination of internal actions. In the oral exam, two theoretical topics are usually given for discussion, and a request may be made for an analysis of the failure of a mechanical component such as a spring, a drive shaft or a gear, for which possible improvements must also be provided. The final mark will be the sum of the marks for the two tests; admission to the oral exam may be granted with a mark of 17 with an asterisk, which means that a good oral performance is expected given the extreme criticality of the written exam. This exam structure is reserved for students whose study plan includes only Module I (Machine Construction A, 6 credits), while for students who opt for Module II (Machine Construction AB, 12 credits), i.e. for the Design curriculum, learning will be assessed in a single final examination for Module II, for which it is (obviously) essential to be able to solve the exercises in Module I. IMPORTANT: For students under the previous teaching system (up to the academic year 24/25), in which only Machine Construction (9 CFU) appeared in the study plan, the examination methods and content remain unchanged (written test, passing grade 18/30, oral test).

sections.Learning objectives: TECNOLOGIA MECCANICA: This course provides the knowledge and ability necessary for analysis of manufacturing processes, production systems and assembly methods for industrial components and products. The primary objective of this course is to develop a level of proficiency sufficient such that students can understand mechanical production processes within an industrial context based on information provided within mechanical and detail drawings. To this end, acquisition of knowledge relating to the following points is necessary: - Information contained within a technical drawing in terms of component geometry, materials, surface finish and dimensional and positioning tolerances; - Issues relating to fulfilment of specific precision requirements during the production cycle and knowledge of measurement tools necessary for quantification; - Foundry and plastic deformation as primary forming processes; - Machining processes utilising machine tools; - Reversible and irreversible joining techniques. To this end, development of the following abilities is necessary: - Study of the primary forming processes of a component; - Determination of the raw material (in terms of dimensions, material and primary production process) for subsequent machining of a component; - Identification of the sequence of operations necessary to create the surfaces making up the component; - Referencing of the component with respect to machine tools utilising appropriate equipment; - Calculation of the forces acting throughout the cutting process and the power absorbed by machine tools. The final objective of this course is for students to develop the ability to correctly plan, from a manufacturing point of view (rational and inexpensive), the process cycles necessary for production of a mechanical component that includes all phases necessary for its creation. sections.Course unit content: The aim of this course is to study manufacturing processes, production systems and assembly methods for industrial components and products. A systematic approach aligned with process modelling is adopted for understanding the principles and mechanisms on which the manufacturing processes are based, and for understanding their capabilities and limitations in terms of achievable functional performance for specific manufactured products, systematic design and planning of the manufacturing process, and integration of the design and production processes. Modelling will be aimed at predicting the influence of process parameters on the resulting outcomes. The course content will be sufficiently analytical for an elementary university course and adequately descriptive for students that have no specific prior knowledge relating to manufacturing processes. The course will consist of lectures and tutorials where exercises will be completed together with the lecturer and discussion of industrial applications will take place.

sections.Assessment methods and criteria: TECNOLOGIA MECCANICA The final exam will verify acquisition of the required knowledge and ability with a 2-hour written exam and an optional oral exam. The written exam comprises 2 questions and 1 exercise. Specifically, candidates will be required to answer: - One theoretical question relating to the explanation of a machine or production process, including schematics, definitions and demonstrations, etc.; - One calculation-based exercise aimed at verifying the candidate’s aptitude in determining quantitative results for the posed question; - A technical/practical exercise relating to formulation of the production cycle for a simple mechanical component based on a quoted technical drawing. The objective of this exercise is to verify the ability of the candidate to choose the most effective and least costly production cycle. To attend the oral exam, it is necessary to achieve a minimum of 18 points in the written exam. The oral exam, which begins with correction of the candidate’s submitted written exam, verifies the competency of the candidate relating to reasoning and discussing of any of the themes covered in the course with the correct terminology and graphical representations. sections.Learning objectives: Knowledge and ability to understand: (I Dublin Descriptor) By the end of the course, the student will have developed and integrated his or her basic knowledge of metallic materials suitable for component fabrication using foundry and additive manufacturing technologies. He/she will have gained awareness of issues related to physical metallurgy, relationships between microstructure and mechanical properties of ferrous and non-ferrous alloys. In particular, by the end of the course the student will be able to select appropriate materials and heat treatments for engineering design. Skills: (II Descriptor: Ability to apply knowledge and understanding) Through lessons and in-class exercises related to all program topics, the student will learn how to apply the knowledge gained in a design context. Autonomy of judgment: (III, IV, V Dublin descriptor) The student should be able to critically understand the characteristics and behavior of matter by evaluating its properties and suitability in relation to the intended applications. He/she will also have to process the relevant data to verify the required performance. Communication skills: (III, IV, V Dublin descriptor) At the end of the course the student should have acquired sufficient language skills, at least as regards the specific technological terminology of the teachings.
sections.Full programme: Basic knowledge of physical metallurgy: Brief introduction to crystallography. Diffusion phenomena correlated to the main heat treatments: I° and II° Fick’s law. Defects within the metallic materials. Phase diagrams: basic characteristics, lever rule, cooling pathways at the thermodynamic equilibrium. Phase diagram of Fe-Fe3C and microstructures. Strengthening mechanisms of the metallic materials. Solidification in conventional and innovative processes. Mechanical characterisation: Tensile test, hardness test, and Charpy impact test. Innovative production process: Metal additive manufacturing: general description, applications and operation of the machine. Process parameters. Advantages and Disadvantages. Steel: Designation. The main microstructures obtained during the main industrial heat treatments. Heat treatments: quenching, annealing, tempering, normalizing. Nitriding and carburizing. Brief description of structural steels, special structural steels, tool steels, and stainless steels. Aluminium alloys: Designations. Main aluminium alloys: microstructure, mechanical properties and applications. Production of aluminium. Main heat treatments and effects induced by cold deformation. Additive Manufacturing. Analysis of application cases and selection criteria for metallic materials: During the course, various application cases will be presented, in which the selection of metallic materials will be carried out based on the required mechanical properties, the component’s function, and the choice of suitable treatments to meet specific operating conditions at room and high temperatures.

sections.Learning objectives: On the basis of a deep knowledge of kinematics, statics and dynamics of mechanical system, the course provides the practical and theorical knowledge required for a proper functional design of machines and their devices.
sections.Prerequisites: Meccanica razionale
sections.Course unit content: Mechanisms assembly. Forces acting on mechanisms. Fundamental concepts of tribology: friction, wearing, lubrication Joints, brakes, clutches. Concepts of kinematics and dynamics and applications to mechanisms. Gears. Transmissions.
sections.Full programme: Historical notes and terminology. Degrees of freedom, Gruebler's and Kutzbach's formulas. Friction: sliding and static friction; cases of friction in prismatic, revolute, thrust, inclined plane, screw-nut pairs; brakes and clutches; rolling friction; cases of idler, driving, and driven wheels; vehicle examples; efficiency, machines in series and in parallel, retrograde motion. Lubrication: Newtonian fluids, mass conservation, constitutive laws, viscosity and units of measurement, Reynolds equation in 2D and 3D, introduction to elastohydrodynamics; hydrodynamic lubrication: applications – fixed and tilting-pad bearings (axial and radial), bushings, Sommerfeld number; hydrostatic lubrication. Kinematics: Galileo’s theorem, instantaneous center of rotation, trajectories, centroids and polodes, Euler-Savary theorem, conjugate profiles, inflection circle, Rivals’ theorem, applications. Linkage systems: analysis and synthesis of four-bar and six-bar linkages, slider-crank mechanisms, Roberts’ theorem, Oldham coupling, Cardan joint, brief notes on other joints (Birfield, tripod, Rzeppa). Cam mechanisms and motion laws. Gears: friction wheels and motivation for toothed gears, involute curve and its properties, pinion and rack, involute spur gears. Chain and belt transmissions. Dynamics of slider-crank mechanisms, substitution masses, balancing of engines with 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, and 12 cylinders.

sections.Learning objectives: The integrated course provides knowledge and skills to understand the operating principles, real characteristics, and performance of major energy systems and prime movers (gas turbines, internal combustion engines, steam plants). By the end of the course, students will be able to: - Understand the fundamentals of energy conversion and the types of fluid machines (drivers and driven). - Analyze real thermodynamic transformations and calculate performance parameters (efficiency, specific fuel consumption). - Assess energy system performance under varying operating conditions. - Critically compare different plant configurations and select fluid machines for specific applications. - Present evaluations and comparisons effectively using graphical and numerical representations.
sections.Prerequisites: Basic knowledge of: - Calculus - Physics - Thermodynamics - Fluid Mechanics - Applied Thermodynamics
sections.Course unit content: - Conventional and renewable energy sources. - Energy systems and fluid machines: types, classification, and components. - Steam plants, gas turbine plants, reciprocating internal combustion engines. - Combined-cycle and cogeneration systems. - Ideal, limiting, and real thermodynamic cycles (Rankine, Joule, Otto, Diesel, Sabathé). - Analysis of real thermodynamic transformations and performance calculations. - Fluid flow in ducts, compression and expansion processes, sonic conditions. - Fluid machines: pumps, compressors, fans, turbines. - Renewable energy conversion: hydroelectric, photovoltaic, bioenergy systems. - Overview of energy cost and utilization factor.
sections.Full programme: - Energy demand, sources, and conversion processes. - Thermodynamic fundamentals: mass and energy balances, ideal gas transformations, property calculations. - Hydrocarbon combustion: stoichiometric air calculation, calorific values. - Thermodynamic cycles: ideal, limiting, and real; work and heat exchange calculations. - Gas turbine plants: components, cycle variants, Joule cycle optimization. - Steam plants: ideal and real cycles, regeneration, reheating, boilers, condensers, cooling towers. - Internal combustion engines: ideal and real cycles, losses, supercharging, performance curves. - Combined-cycle and cogeneration systems: performance indices (IRE, PES). - Renewable energy conversion: hydroelectric systems, photovoltaic systems, bioenergy. - Fluid machines: classification, similarity laws, characteristic curves, cavitation, compressors, fans. - Quantitative analysis of performance and thermodynamic parameters.

Facchini, *Exercises on Energy Systems*, Esculapio, 2016. - Lecture notes and slides available on Elly platform.
sections.Teaching methods: - Lectures supported by slides and schematic diagrams. - Numerical exercises to apply theoretical concepts and develop calculation skills. - Presentation of quantitative examples and calculation procedures. - Teaching materials available on Elly platform.
sections.Assessment methods and criteria: - **Written exam**: one numerical exercise, five structured questions, and two open questions (exercise must be correct and minimum score required on structured questions). - **Oral exam**: two questions on theory and practical applications (each question must score at least 18/30). Final grade is the average of the two oral questions. - Evaluation focuses on critical thinking, clarity of presentation, ability to correlate topics, and numerical problem-solving.

sections.Learning objectives: This module aims to provide in-depth knowledge and skills (i.e., the ability to apply knowledge) necessary to assess the real-world operating characteristics and performance of energy systems, with particular emphasis on most commonly used the power plants (gas turbines, Internal Combustion Engines, and steam plants). To develop deeper skills in assessing the performance of any thermal power plant for energy generation and conversion, students are required to demonstrate the achievement of the following objectives by the end of the module. Knowledge and understanding: At the end of the course, students will be able to understand the real operating characteristics and performance of power generation systems and the main prime movers used today. They will also have acquired specific knowledge for assessing real thermodynamic transformations, for calculating thermodynamic parameters and heat and work exchanges with reference to real cases. They will therefore be familiar with the problems, limitations, advantages, and disadvantages of the considered power plants and their main components in real operating conditions. Applying knowledge and understanding: The student will be able to calculate the performance parameters of engines, with particular reference to efficiency and specific fuel consumption. They will also be able to define the behavior of real thermodynamic transformations occurring in power plants and their components in order to qualitatively and quantitatively evaluate the thermodynamic states and real transormations, as well as identify solutions to improve performance. Making judgments: The student will have tools and knowledge needed to critically evaluate and compare different solutions for implementing real energy conversion processes in power systems, taking into account thereal behavior of transformations and processes, while also considering possible alternatives. Communication skills: The student will gain the tools required to effectively present evaluations and comparisons of different solutions for implementing energy conversion processes in power plants, through both graphical and numerical representations of the real thermodynamic transformations and cycles, as well as the main performance parameters commonly used. Learning skills: Using the knowledge acquired in the course, students will be able to independently get information, characteristics, and technical data on Energy Systems that can be studied and/or available on the market, thus improving own skills on the solutions proposed and/or applied for the implementation and management of Energy Systems.
sections.Prerequisites: Basic knowledge of fundamentals of Mathematics, Physics, Thermodynamics and Fluid Mechanics is required.
sections.Course unit content: Energy Systems and Fluid Machines: classification and components. Review of Thermodynamics. Fundamental equations: mass and energy conservation; momentum and moment of momentum equations. Application to fluid flow in fixed and moving channels. Ideal, Limit, and Real thermodynamic cycles. Overview of Energy costs and utilization factors. Compressible Fluid Machines. Compression and expansion processes on thermodynamic diagrams; compression and expansion efficiencies. Total and stagnation quantities. Fluid Flow in fixed channels: converging channels, converging-diverging channels. Velocity and pressure trends, sonic and choking conditions. Steam Engines. Real Cycles: thermodynamic transformations in real Rankine cycles with saturated and superheated steam; performance calculation for reheated and regenerated steam plants in real operation. Steam generators: types and schemes; efficiency. Superheaters and economizers. Air preheaters. Condenser and cooling towers. Reciprocating internal combustion engines (ICEs). Limit thermodynamic cycles: an overview of calculation methodology. Real thermodynamic cycles: trends of real transformations and main causes of deviation from the ideal case. Indicated cycle and calculation of effective power in internal combustion engines. Mean effective pressure. Volumetric efficiency. Overview of combustion processes. Air and fuel supply processes in ICEs. Mechanical supercharging and turbocharging. Characteristic curves. Gas turbines: thermodynamic processes in the Joule cycle in the limit and real cases. Real thermodynamic cycles on the (h, s) and (T, s) diagrams; effective specific work, effective power, and thermodynamic efficiency in limit and real Joule cycle. Effect of compression ratio and maximum cycle temperature. Turbine inlet temperature (TIT) and air-fuel ratio: effects on efficiency. Optimization of the real Joule cycle with reference to specific work and efficiency.
sections.Full programme: Energy Systems and Fluid Machines: characteristics and classification. Internal and External Combustion Plants. Components of Energy Systems. Thermodynamics reminders: closed and open systems, Heat Exchangers and Fluid Machinery. Fundamental equations: mass and energy conservation; momentum and moment of momentum equations. Application of conservation equations to fluid flow in fixed and moving channels. Thermodynamic cycles and pseudo-cycles: thermodynamic transformations, work and heat exchange calculation. Ideal, Limit, and Real Cycles. Overview on energy cost and utilization coefficient. Compressible Fluid Machines. Compression and expansion transformations on thermodynamic diagrams; real and ideal transformations. Compression and expansion efficiencies, recovery and counter-recovery phenomena. Intercooled and post-combustion compression. total and stagnation quantities. Fluid flow in fixed-wall ducts: converging ducts, converging-diverging ducts. Evaluation of velocity and pressure trends with a 1-D approach. Sonic and choking conditions. Valves and pressure reducers. Notes on fluid flow in moving channels. Steam power plants: overview of the most common system configurations. Real cycles for steam power plants: transformations in real Rankine cycles with saturated and superheated steam. Regeneration and reheating: real thermodynamic cycles on the (h, s) and (T, s) diagrams. Performance calculation of simple, reheated, and regenerated steam power plants in real situations. Steam generators: types and basic schemes. Steam generator efficiency: direct and indirect calculations. Superheaters and economizers. Air preheaters. The condenser and cooling towers. The deaerator. Reciprocating internal combustion engines (ICEs). Review of operating principles and fundamental components. Limit thermodynamic cycles: an overview of calculation methodology. Real thermodynamic cycles: evolution of real transformations and main causes of deviation from the ideal case. Time losses, heat exchange, pressure drops through intake and exhaust valves and throttle valve. Indicated cycle and calculation of effective power in ICE. Mean effective pressure. Volumetric efficiency. Overview of combustion processes in spark-ignition and Diesel engines. Air and fuel supply processes in ICEs: intake and exhaust systems and polar diagram of ideal and real valves timing. Mechanical supercharging and turbocharging. Characteristic curves of internal combustion engines. Gas turbines: an overview of the most common configurations. Real cycles for gas turbine power plants: thermodynamic transformations in the Joule cycle in the limit and real cases. Real thermodynamic cycles on the (h, s) and (T, s) diagrams. Calculation of effective specific work, effective power, and thermodynamic efficiency in limit and real Joule cycle. Effect of compression ratio and maximum cycle temperature. Calculation of turbine inlet temperature (TIT) and air-fuel ratio values: effects on efficiency and problems arising from material resistance. Introduction to blade cooling. Introduction to combustion chamber geometry. Optimization of the real Joule cycle with reference to specific work and efficiency.

sections.Teaching methods: Teaching activities will be developed through classroom lectures, during which the course topics will be addressed both theoretically, to promote understanding of the topics presented (connecting them where appropriate with the student's existing knowledge), and practically, through the presentation of quantitative examples of specific power plants and the calculation procedures that lead to the numerical evaluation of the plants real operating characteristics, performance parameters, and the real thermodynamic transformations. The practical applications presented will be aimed at enabling students to acquire the necessary familiarity with units of measurement, the quantitative calculation of real thermodynamic transformations, and the performance evaluation of the considered power plants. The activities described will be primarily developed in the classroom, with the aim of allowing students to actively follow the procedures and methodologies employed. The teacher is available for clarifications and explanations by appointment (to be arranged via email) both in person and online (through the Teams platform).
sections.Assessment methods and criteria: The assessment of learning is carried out through the final exam only, which ensures the acquisition of knowledge and skills (i.e. acquisition of learning outcomes) through an oral interview. The oral exam consists in two questions on the topics of the course and on the application of the theory to original problems: in particular, critical thinking skills, presentation skills, the ability to correlate the topics covered and to perform numerical calculations to quantitatively evaluate parameters and quantities of interest in specific problems will be evaluated. Each question is assessed on a scale from 0 to 30. To pass the exam a partial score of at least 18/30 IS REQUIRED FOR BOTH QUESTIONS. sections.Learning objectives: Knowledge and understanding: At the end of this course the student should know the basics of machine design. He should gain understanding of the many factors affecting the design of mechanical parts with special regards to safety and reliability. He should be familiar with design schemes and checks required to analyze machine parts. Applying knowledge and understanding: He should be able to design a mechanical part on the basis of suitable material and process selection, load analysis and functional requirements. He should be able to select from catalogues the main mechanical components found in machines. He should be able to draw and dimension the part for production. Making judgments: By the end of the course the student should be able to critically analyze machines and mechanical components and to their functions and requisites. Communication skills: The student should be able to clearly present the functioning of mechanical devices and the design issues involved.
sections.Prerequisites: It will be very useful to recall the following concepts: - Physics 1: units of measurement, forces and moments in a plane, vector representation, graphical resolution of static equilibrium - Machine drawing: views, dimensioning, dimensional and geometric tolerances, bearing assembly - Mechanical technology: machining technologies, heat treatment of steel - Metallurgy: metal alloys and their applications, mechanical testing - Structural science: beam theory, mass geometry, de Saint-Venant theory - Rational mechanics: kinematics, rigid body dynamics, kinematic mechanisms, and force calculations
sections.Course unit content: The course covers the principles of mechanical design applied to machine components, starting with the strength characteristics of commonly used materials and the concept of safety. It then introduces methods and models for the schematization of acting loads and the calculation and sizing of components. A key aspect is the introduction to strength testing under fatigue loads.
sections.Full programme: Introduction to Construction Design, Safety, Factor of Safety with Statistical Reliability Concepts, Technical Standards, Mechanical Testing of Materials, Tensile, Hardness, Impact, Fatigue, Fracture Testing, Metallic Materials (Steel, Cast Iron, Aluminum, Magnesium, Titanium Alloys), Non-Metallic Materials (Polymers and Ceramics), Manufacturing Technologies, Selection Criteria. Load Analysis, Equilibrium, Application of the Beam Model in Mechanics, Normal Force, Bending, Shear, and Torsion. Stresses and Strains. Mohr Circles. Principal Stresses, Strength Criteria (Tresca, Von Mises, Rankine), Ductility and Brittleness. Compressive Buckling and Eulerian Loading. Stiffness. Highly Curvatured Beams. Notched Geometries, Nominal and Local Stresses, Stress Concentration Factor Kt. Conformal and Non-Conformal Contact, Specific Contact Pressure, Hertzian Theory, Stresses in Contact between Elementary Bodies. Thermal Expansion. Fatigue of Metallic Materials, Characteristics of the Phenomenon, Fatigue Testing, Stress Limit fatigue, S/N curves, fatigue parameter estimates, influence factors, mean stress effect, fatigue damage accumulation, multiaxial stress effect, notch sensitivity, Notch effect factor Kf. Contact fatigue, pitting, fretting.

sections.Teaching methods: Course topics are presented through lectures and numerical exercises carried out in the classroom. Problems are proposed to be carried out at home with subsequent discussion in the classroom. Groups of students are also stimulated to analyse and study a real mechanical device.
sections.Assessment methods and criteria: The examination consists of a written test, which must be passed with a minimum score of 18/30, followed by an oral test. In the written exam, students will be required to solve an exercise concerning the design of a simple mechanical system, such as a lifting device, a pressure vessel or a drive shaft, considering the main factors that determine the safety of the system, such as the choice of the most suitable materials, durability, or compliance with regulations. In order to pass the written exam, it is essential to correctly perform the load analysis by means of static resolution and the determination of internal actions. In the oral exam, two theoretical topics are usually given for discussion, and a request may be made for an analysis of the failure of a mechanical component such as a spring, a drive shaft or a gear, for which possible improvements must also be provided. The final mark will be the sum of the marks for the two tests; admission to the oral exam may be granted with a mark of 17 with an asterisk, which means that a good oral performance is expected given the extreme criticality of the written exam. This exam structure is reserved for students whose study plan includes only Module I (Machine Construction A, 6 credits), while for students who opt for Module II (Machine Construction AB, 12 credits), i.e. for the Design curriculum, learning will be assessed in a single final examination for Module II, for which it is (obviously) essential to be able to solve the exercises in Module I. sections.Learning objectives: TECNOLOGIA MECCANICA: This course provides the knowledge and ability necessary for analysis of manufacturing processes, production systems and assembly methods for industrial components and products. The primary objective of this course is to develop a level of proficiency sufficient such that students can understand mechanical production processes within an industrial context based on information provided within mechanical and detail drawings. To this end, acquisition of knowledge relating to the following points is necessary: - Information contained within a technical drawing in terms of component geometry, materials, surface finish and dimensional and positioning tolerances; - Issues relating to fulfilment of specific precision requirements during the production cycle and knowledge of measurement tools necessary for quantification; - Foundry and plastic deformation as primary forming processes; - Machining processes utilising machine tools; - Reversible and irreversible joining techniques. To this end, development of the following abilities is necessary: - Study of the primary forming processes of a component; - Determination of the raw material (in terms of dimensions, material and primary production process) for subsequent machining of a component; - Identification of the sequence of operations necessary to create the surfaces making up the component; - Referencing of the component with respect to machine tools utilising appropriate equipment; - Calculation of the forces acting throughout the cutting process and the power absorbed by machine tools. The final objective of this course is for students to develop the ability to correctly plan, from a manufacturing point of view (rational and inexpensive), the process cycles necessary for production of a mechanical component that includes all phases necessary for its creation. sections.Course unit content: The aim of this course is to study manufacturing processes, production systems and assembly methods for industrial components and products. A systematic approach aligned with process modelling is adopted for understanding the principles and mechanisms on which the manufacturing processes are based, and for understanding their capabilities and limitations in terms of achievable functional performance for specific manufactured products, systematic design and planning of the manufacturing process, and integration of the design and production processes. Modelling will be aimed at predicting the influence of process parameters on the resulting outcomes. The course content will be sufficiently analytical for an elementary university course and adequately descriptive for students that have no specific prior knowledge relating to manufacturing processes. The course will consist of lectures and tutorials where exercises will be completed together with the lecturer and discussion of industrial applications will take place.
sections.Full programme: TECNOLOGIA MECCANICA: Introduction Basics and classification of manufacturing processes. Modelling transformations taking place during manufacturing processes, including material, energy and information flow. Relationships between product and manufacturing process; product design and process planning. Manufacturing process selection criteria. sections.Assessment methods and criteria: TECNOLOGIA MECCANICA The final exam will verify acquisition of the required knowledge and ability with a 2-hour written exam and an optional oral exam. sections.Learning objectives: Knowledge and understanding: by means of frontal lessons, the student acquires the method and knowledge required to describe, understand and design the industrial production and storage systems, to define their maintenance criteria; student learns how to efficiently use project management tools by means of statistic basics provided. The student will learn the structure and the operating principle of industrial plants in terms of: organization and management of the transformation of raw material into finished product, reliability of complex systems, role of human resources and industrial automation, production flows and layout, KPI and performance measurements.Applying knowledge and understanding: Through practical classroom exercises connected to some important topics, students learn how to apply the acquired knowledge in a real context of design, as well as in multidisciplinary or non-familiar areas.In particular, the student will have to apply the acquired knowledge to the industrialization of a production process, starting from the feasibility study, defining the best production structure and management, assessing the possibility of using automated operations to replace manual ones and controlling process through KPIs.Making judgements: The student must be able to understand and critically evaluate the main production systems (forced and not-forced technological processes, production or assembly, manual or automated); using acquired knowledge, he will have to analyze existing systems and assess their performances and adequacy, assess the impact of strategic, planning and operational decisions, measure plant performances.Communication skills: Through the front lessons and the assistance of the teacher, the student acquires the specific vocabulary inherent to the production plants. At the end of the course, the student is expected to be able to communicate the main contents of the course, both written and orally, such as ideas, engineering issues and related solutions. The student must communicate his knowledge through appropriate tools, so numerical problems are solved using common methods in the industry such as tables, diagrams, flow charts, and numerical spreadsheets.Learning skills: The student who has attended the course will be able to deepen his knowledge of production plants through the autonomous consultation of specialized books, scientific or divulgative journals, even outside the topics explained during lectures.

sections.Course unit content: The course aims to provide the students with the general criteria for designing and realizing the main production plants, which are complex systems consisting of the technological plants, utilities and facilities that contribute to the achievement of the economic goal. Therefore, the content covered during the lessons in the first part of the course concerns the classification of production plants, with and without a constrained technological cycle, and manual and automated manufacturing and assembly processes. The main performance indicators for monitoring the efficiency of industrial plants are defined. Project management tools and reliability theory for the maintenance of production systems are also introduced. The second part of the course assesses the impact of automation on these processes, both from a control and predictive maintenance perspective, describes material handling and product storage systems, and introduces some methods for sizing storage systems.

sections.Teaching methods: The course counts 12 CFUs (one CFU, University Credits equals one ECTS credit and represents the workload of a student during educational activities aimed at passing the exams), which corresponds to 96 hours of lectures. The lectures will be organized in presence. The didactic activities are composed of frontal lessons alternating with exercises. During the frontal lessons, the course topics are proposed from the theoretical and design point of view.During classroom exercises students are allowed to bring their own computers and tablets, and they will apply theoretical knowledge to an exercise, a real case study, or a project.If conditions are favorable, seminars are held by managers of multinational corporations who report concrete experiences in real case studies.The slides and notes used to support the lessons will be uploaded to the Elly Platform.Notes, slides, spreadsheets, tables, and all shared material are part of the didactic material. For non-attending students, it is important to stay up-to-date on the course through the Elly platform, the only communication tool used for direct teacher / student contact.On this platform, day by day, the topics discussed in the lesson are pointed out and registered, providing the students with an index of the contents for the final exam.
sections.Assessment methods and criteria: Verification of the knowledge takes place through a written test based on open questions, lasting 2.5 hours. The test usually consists of 11/12 questions that may relate to theoretical content, demonstrations, and exercises that have been done during the course; theoretical demonstrations have a weight of 1.0; Plant design and technical drawings weight 1.5; Exercises weight 1.8. The final vote is calculated by assigning a mark in the range 0-30 for each question and then performing the weighted average of the individual evaluations, with final ceiling to the next unit; the test is exceeded if it reaches a score of at least 18 points. “30 cum laude” is given to students who achieve the highest score on each item and use precise vocabulary. The examination will be carried out in presence, if possible, otherwise it will be carried out online, with similar or suitably adapted methods.

sections.Learning objectives: Knowledge and ability to understand: (I Dublin Descriptor) By the end of the course, the student will have developed and integrated his or her basic knowledge of metallic materials suitable for component fabrication using foundry and additive manufacturing technologies. He/she will have gained awareness of issues related to physical metallurgy, relationships between microstructure and mechanical properties of ferrous and non-ferrous alloys. In particular, by the end of the course the student will be able to select appropriate materials and heat treatments for engineering design. Skills: (II Descriptor: Ability to apply knowledge and understanding) Through lessons and in-class exercises related to all program topics, the student will learn how to apply the knowledge gained in a design context. Autonomy of judgment: (III, IV, V Dublin descriptor) The student should be able to critically understand the characteristics and behavior of matter by evaluating its properties and suitability in relation to the intended applications. He/she will also have to process the relevant data to verify the required performance. Communication skills: (III, IV, V Dublin descriptor) At the end of the course the student should have acquired sufficient language skills, at least as regards the specific technological terminology of the teachings.
sections.Full programme: Basic knowledge of physical metallurgy: Brief introduction to crystallography. Diffusion phenomena correlated to the main heat treatments: I° and II° Fick’s law. Defects within the metallic materials. Phase diagrams: basic characteristics, lever rule, cooling pathways at the thermodynamic equilibrium. Phase diagram of Fe-Fe3C and microstructures. Strengthening mechanisms of the metallic materials. Solidification in conventional and innovative processes. Mechanical characterisation: Tensile test, hardness test, and Charpy impact test. Innovative production process: Metal additive manufacturing: general description, applications and operation of the machine. Process parameters. Advantages and Disadvantages. Steel: Designation. The main microstructures obtained during the main industrial heat treatments. Heat treatments: quenching, annealing, tempering, normalizing. Nitriding and carburizing. Brief description of structural steels, special structural steels, tool steels, and stainless steels. Aluminium alloys: Designations. Main aluminium alloys: microstructure, mechanical properties and applications. Production of aluminium. Main heat treatments and effects induced by cold deformation. Additive Manufacturing. Analysis of application cases and selection criteria for metallic materials: During the course, various application cases will be presented, in which the selection of metallic materials will be carried out based on the required mechanical properties, the component’s function, and the choice of suitable treatments to meet specific operating conditions at room and high temperatures.

sections.Learning objectives: Knowledge and understanding: At the end of this course the student should know the basics of machine design. He should gain understanding of the many factors affecting the design of mechanical parts with special regards to safety and reliability. He should be familiar with design schemes and checks required to analyze machine parts. Applying knowledge and understanding: He should be able to design a mechanical part on the basis of suitable material and process selection, load analysis and functional requirements. He should be able to select from catalogues the main mechanical components found in machines. He should be able to draw and dimension the part for production. Making judgments: By the end of the course the student should be able to critically analyze machines and mechanical components and to their functions and requisites. Communication skills: The student should be able to clearly present the functioning of mechanical devices and the design issues involved.
sections.Prerequisites: Physics 1: Forces and moments in space, their vector representation and vector sum/difference Machine drawing: rules for drawing components and parts, dimensioning, understanding the drawing of parts and assemblies Strength of materials/Solid mechanics: beam theory, calculating constraint reactions and internal forces, geometry of masses, stress calculations, resistance criteria Applied physiscs: kinematics and dynamics of rigid bodies Metallurgy: naming steels and light alloys (symbols and meaning), material selection criteria in relation to the manufacturing process Mechanical technology: manufacturing process in relation to the type and shape of the mechanical component to be manufactured
sections.Course unit content: The course covers the principles of mechanical design applied to machine components, starting with the strength characteristics of commonly used materials and the concept of safety. It then introduces methods and models for the schematization of acting loads and the calculation and sizing of components. A key aspect is the introduction to strength testing under fatigue loads. The course will cover the main mechanical components.
sections.Full programme: Introduction to Construction Design, Safety, Factor of Safety with Statistical Reliability Concepts, Technical Standards, Mechanical Testing of Materials, Tensile, Hardness, Impact, Fatigue, Fracture Testing, Metallic Materials (Steel, Cast Iron, Aluminum, Magnesium, Titanium Alloys), Non-Metallic Materials (Polymers and Ceramics), Manufacturing Technologies, Selection Criteria. Load Analysis, Equilibrium, Application of the Beam Model in Mechanics, Normal Force, Bending, Shear, and Torsion. Stresses and Strains. Mohr Circles. Principal Stresses, Strength Criteria (Tresca, Von Mises, Rankine), Ductility and Brittleness. Compressive Buckling and Eulerian Loading. Stiffness. Highly Curvatured Beams. Notched Geometries, Nominal and Local Stresses, Stress Concentration Factor Kt. Conformal and Non-Conformal Contact, Specific Contact Pressure, Hertzian Theory, Stresses in Contact between Elementary Bodies. Thermal Expansion. sections.Learning objectives: Knowledge and understanding: by means of frontal lessons, the student acquires the method and knowledge required to describe, understand and design the industrial production and storage systems, to define their maintenance criteria; student learns how to efficiently use project management tools by means of statistic basics provided. The student will learn the structure and the operating principle of industrial plants in terms of: organization and management of the transformation of raw material into finished product, reliability of complex systems, role of human resources and industrial automation, production flows and layout, KPI and performance measurements.Applying knowledge and understanding: Through practical classroom exercises connected to some important topics, students learn how to apply the acquired knowledge in a real context of design, as well as in multidisciplinary or non-familiar areas.In particular, the student will have to apply the acquired knowledge to the industrialization of a production process, starting from the feasibility study, defining the best production structure and management, assessing the possibility of using automated operations to replace manual ones and controlling process through KPIs.Making judgements: The student must be able to understand and critically evaluate the main production systems (forced and not-forced technological processes, production or assembly, manual or automated); using acquired knowledge, he will have to analyze existing systems and assess their performances and adequacy, assess the impact of strategic, planning and operational decisions, measure plant performances.Communication skills: Through the front lessons and the assistance of the teacher, the student acquires the specific vocabulary inherent to the production plants. At the end of the course, the student is expected to be able to communicate the main contents of the course, both written and orally, such as ideas, engineering issues and related solutions. The student must communicate his knowledge through appropriate tools, so numerical problems are solved using common methods in the industry such as tables, diagrams, flow charts, and numerical spreadsheets.Learning skills: The student who has attended the course will be able to deepen his knowledge of production plants through the autonomous consultation of specialized books, scientific or divulgative journals, even outside the topics explained during lectures.

sections.Learning objectives: On the basis of a deep knowledge of kinematics, statics and dynamics of mechanical system, the course provides the practical and theorical knowledge required for a proper functional design of machines and their devices.

sections.Course unit content: Mechanisms assembly. Forces acting on mechanisms. Fundamental concepts of tribology: friction, wearing, lubrication Joints, brakes, clutches. Concepts of kinematics and dynamics and applications to mechanisms. Gears.
sections.Full programme: Historical notes and terminology. Degrees of freedom, Gruebler's and Kutzbach's formulas. Friction: sliding and static friction; cases of friction in prismatic, revolute, thrust, inclined plane, screw-nut pairs; brakes and clutches; rolling friction; cases of idler, driving, and driven wheels; vehicle examples; efficiency, machines in series and in parallel, retrograde motion. Lubrication: Newtonian fluids, mass conservation, constitutive laws, viscosity and units of measurement, Reynolds equation in 2D and 3D, introduction to elastohydrodynamics; hydrodynamic lubrication: applications – fixed and tilting-pad bearings (axial and radial), bushings, Sommerfeld number; hydrostatic lubrication. Kinematics: Galileo’s theorem, instantaneous center of rotation, trajectories, centroids and polodes, Euler-Savary theorem, conjugate profiles, inflection circle, Rivals’ theorem, applications. Linkage systems: analysis and synthesis of four-bar and six-bar linkages, slider-crank mechanisms, Roberts’ theorem, Oldham coupling, Cardan joint, brief notes on other joints (Birfield, tripod, Rzeppa). Cam mechanisms and motion laws. Gears: friction wheels and motivation for toothed gears, involute curve and its properties, pinion and rack, involute spur gears. Chain and belt transmissions. Dynamics of slider-crank mechanisms, substitution masses, balancing of engines with 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, and 12 cylinders.

sections.Learning objectives: TECNOLOGIA MECCANICA: This course provides the knowledge and ability necessary for analysis of manufacturing processes, production systems and assembly methods for industrial components and products. The primary objective of this course is to develop a level of proficiency sufficient such that students can understand mechanical production processes within an industrial context based on information provided within mechanical and detail drawings. To this end, acquisition of knowledge relating to the following points is necessary: - Information contained within a technical drawing in terms of component geometry, materials, surface finish and dimensional and positioning tolerances; - Issues relating to fulfilment of specific precision requirements during the production cycle and knowledge of measurement tools necessary for quantification; - Foundry and plastic deformation as primary forming processes; - Machining processes utilising machine tools; - Reversible and irreversible joining techniques. To this end, development of the following abilities is necessary: - Study of the primary forming processes of a component; - Determination of the raw material (in terms of dimensions, material and primary production process) for subsequent machining of a component; - Identification of the sequence of operations necessary to create the surfaces making up the component; - Referencing of the component with respect to machine tools utilising appropriate equipment; - Calculation of the forces acting throughout the cutting process and the power absorbed by machine tools. The final objective of this course is for students to develop the ability to correctly plan, from a manufacturing point of view (rational and inexpensive), the process cycles necessary for production of a mechanical component that includes all phases necessary for its creation. sections.Course unit content: The aim of this course is to study manufacturing processes, production systems and assembly methods for industrial components and products. A systematic approach aligned with process modelling is adopted for understanding the principles and mechanisms on which the manufacturing processes are based, and for understanding their capabilities and limitations in terms of achievable functional performance for specific manufactured products, systematic design and planning of the manufacturing process, and integration of the design and production processes. Modelling will be aimed at predicting the influence of process parameters on the resulting outcomes. The course content will be sufficiently analytical for an elementary university course and adequately descriptive for students that have no specific prior knowledge relating to manufacturing processes. The course will consist of lectures and tutorials where exercises will be completed together with the lecturer and discussion of industrial applications will take place.

sections.Course unit content: 1. Curves. 2. Vector valued functions: continuity and limits. 3. Differential calculus in several variables. 4. Multiple integrals. 5. Differential equations.
sections.Full programme: 1. Curves. Preliminaries (linear algebra; polar coordinates and planar rotations). Parametric curves (velocity and acceleration; regular curves). Curve in polar coordinates. Length of a curve (curves in polar form; cartesian curves; piecewise regular curves). Repamareterization (cylindrical helix). Curvature and torsion. 2. Vector valued functions: continuity and limits. Real functions of two real variables (level sets). Polar, spherical, and cylindrical coordinates (vector valued functions). Elemens of topology. Continuous functions (intermediate values theorem; Lipschitz and unuiformly continuous functions; distance function to a set). Integral of a function along a curve (curvilinear integral of functions and of vector fields; integral on the oriented boundary of planar sets). Quadratic forms (Sylvester criterion). Limits of functions. 3. Differential calculus in several variables. Partial derivates (Jacobian matrix; a relevant counterexample; directional derivatives). Differentiable functions (infinitesimals and Taylor expansions; diﬀerential; maximum slope direction; total differential theorem; vector valued differentiable functions). Operations with partial derivatives. Higher order derivatives (Schwarz theorem; Taylor formula). Local extremes (Fermat theorem; nature of stationary points; sufficient conditions in two and three dimensions). Contrained extremes (Lagrange multipliers method in two variables). Surfaces in Euclidean space (Lagrange multipliers method in three variables). Potentials and curvilinear integrals (curl-free vector fields). 4. Multiple integrals. Integral over a rectangular box (reduction formulas for double integrals). Integration on a normal set. Change of variables (polar coordinates; an improper integral; implicit transformations). Integrals in three dimensions (integration by wires, integration by layers; change of variables). 5. Diﬀerential equations. Preliminar examples. Cauchy problem for equations and systems. Existence, extendability, and uniqueness of solutions. First order differential equations (first order linear equations; separable variable equations; Bernoulli equations). Second order linear equations with constant coeﬃcients (variation of constants). Linear systems with constant coefficients.

sections.Learning objectives: By means of the frontal lessons, the student should be independently able to understand and to schematize by means of mathematical models simple phisical phenomena involving particles and rigid bodies. Moreover, the student should acquire the aptitude to learn, with critical mind, the theachings typical of the Mechanical Engineering degree.
sections.Prerequisites: There are no mandatory propedeuticities, but Mathematical Analysis, Geometry and Phisics I are strongly recommended.
sections.Course unit content: Rational (or Theoretical) Mechanics is the science that studies the general laws of mechanical motions of material bodies (particles, rigid bodies) and establishes general procedures and methods for solving problems involving such motions. Being a mathematical science, Rational Mechanics deals not with real phisical objects but with abstract schematized conceptions. Consequently, Rational Mechanics il the link between the pure mathematics courses (Mathematical Analisys, Geometry) and the courses of engineering contents (expecially, Applied Mechanics). It is customary to divide the course into three basic parts: Statics (the study of the rules of composition of forces and the conditions of equilibrium of rigid bodies), Kinematics (the study of motions of bodies from the geometric viewpoint alone, without reference to the forces acting on the bodies) and Dynamics (the study of the relationships between the motions of material bodies and the forces acting on them) . In particular, we emphasize the plane kinematics of the rigid bodies, and the dynamics of the one-dimensional mechanical systems.
sections.Full programme: Free vectors theory - geometry of the plane curves - kinematics of the element - kinematics of the rigid body - relative kinematics - rigid plane motiond - polar curves - statics and dynamics of the element - cardinal equations - applied vectors theory - one-dimensional mechanical systems (Lagrange's equations) - statics and dynamics of the rigid body - statics and dynamics of the articulate systems.

sections.Learning objectives: This course aims at teaching the fundamental knowledge for studying the functional and constructive features of mechanical devices, by means of drafted representations that comply with technical standards, and according to their choice as a consequence of the production process. The course goal is to provide students with the necessary awareness and knowledge to create and interpret technical drawings for both individual parts and assemblies. Specifically, students are expected to acquire the following fundamental skills:: (i) to understand the theory and basic notions of technical drawing and its related standards (ii) to know the main elements and modules of machines and mechanical systems (iii) to draft technical drawings based on their application and the manufacturing processes needed to realize the parts (iv) to compare design alternatives for mechanical systems based on external requirements (v) to develop adequate independence in the evaluation of mechanical systems for a correct design and representation (vi) to develop a fluency in the representation of mechanical systems (both in hand-sketching and with the help of software tools) (vii) to be able to provide new concepts and design solutions for components and assemblies considering the changing external requirements
sections.Prerequisites: None
sections.Course unit content: At the beginning of the course, there is an introduction to the basics of technical drafting, such as geometric constructions, orthogonal projections, axonometries, representations of surfaces, sections, rotations, and reflections. After some forewords about materials used in mechanical applications, metrology, and machining, this course thoroughly deals with typical issues of mechanical drafting, considering most used standards, conventional representations, and most common principles of dimensioning. Relationships with production and control processes are carefully taken into consideration. Further topics are dimensional tolerances, geometric tolerances, and surface roughness. There is a thorough analysis of separable joints (by means of threaded parts), fixed joints (welding, soldering), and elastic connections (by means of springs). Furthermore, couplings used for torque transmission from the shaft to other elements are analyzed (keys, cotter, splined shaft, pins). Other topics are bearings and seals, along with several application examples, with special emphasis on the methodology which lead to their choice and mounting. The course deals also with mechanical transmission devices, such as shafts, joints, belts, chains, and gears.
sections.Full programme: 1) Machine drawing basis: standards and standardization authorities, standard sizes of drawing sheets, basic line types and interpretation, font heights and types, drawing scales, sheet layout and title block, drawing types (assembly and part), bill-of-materials. 2) Axonometric projection: classification. Isometric, Dimetric, and Cabinet projections. 3) Isometric views: European system (first angle projection), American system (third angle projection). Symbols. Selection of Views. Designation and Relative Positions of Views. Development of Missing Views. Conventional representation. 4) Sectional views: definition, Conventional representation, Position of sectional views. Sectional view types: Full Section, Half Section, Local Section. Hatching of sections. 5) Dimensioning: definitions (dimension line, projection line, termination, value of the dimension). Special indications (Diameters, Chords, Archs, Angles, Radii, Chamfers, Tapered, etc.). Arrangement of dimensions (chain dimensioning, parallel dimensioning, combined dimensioning, co-ordinate dimensioning). Functional dimensioning, Technological dimensioning. Examples. 6) Materials and technologies: chipping, grinding, milling, refining, etc. Introduction to “Geometrical Product Specifications” (GPS). 7) Limits, Dimensional tolerances, and fits: Fundamental tolerances, Fundamental deviations, Method of placing limit dimensioning, Standards followed in industry (ISO), Fits (clearance, transition, interference). Indicating geometrical tolerances on the drawings. Examples. 9) Surface roughness: Introduction and definition. Surface roughness parameters. sections.Prerequisites: Basic knowledge of calculus, linear algebra and physics.
sections.Course unit content: The course aims to provide a unified treatment of the main aspects of the mechanical behavior of structures, in the linear elastic range. The first part of the course is devoted to the evaluation of the static schemes and strain in elastic solids under assigned external actions. Structural theories for beams will subsequently be addressed. The topics covered are more specifically as follows. • Basic principles of mechanics. Fundamental equations of statics. • Constraints, Free Body Diagrams, calculation of constraint reactions. • Shear force and bending moment diagrams in slender beams. • Stress and strain. Linear elastic constitutive relation. Mohr’s graphical representation. Strength criteria. • De Saint Venant problem. Normal stress. Twist. Simple bending. Shear. • Solution of statically undetermined structures. • Instability phenomena, Euler beam. The application aspect is taken care of through the introduction of a large number of solved examples and exercises.
